CARC 197 (precertification/authorization/notification absent): the claim was submitted without an authorization that this payer requires; either a workflow failure or a policy change making authorization newly required.
CARC 18 (duplicate claim) or CARC 97 (payment included in another service): your billing team is submitting the same claim twice, or the payer considers a billed service bundled into another.
CARC 29 (the time limit for filing has expired): the claim was submitted after the payer's timely filing deadline. This is a charge entry lag problem.
In a typical practice with eight to twelve contracted payers, the top two denial-generating payers account for 60 to 70 percent of total denial volume.
Ten re-worked denials per biller per day is sustainable. Fifty is not.
Clean claim rate measures the percentage of claims that pass through your clearinghouse and are accepted by the payer on the first submission: no rejections, no missing information, no edit failures.
A rejection happens before adjudication: the clearinghouse or payer finds a technical or structural problem and returns the claim without processing it. A denial happens after adjudication.
Authorization failures generate a specific and highly visible rejection class that is entirely preventable when the authorization workflow is functioning correctly.
Invalid diagnosis code: the ICD-10 code is missing a required digit, is an invalid code for the date of service, or is a header code that cannot be used on a claim.
Every rendering provider, billing provider, and referring provider in the system should have an NPI that matches the CMS NPPES database and the enrollment records at each contracted payer.
Re-submitting a rejected claim with the same error generates a second rejection and, at some payers, triggers a duplicate claim flag that complicates the eventual correct submission.
If your practice management system is reporting a clean claim rate above 95% but your denial rate is above 8%, those two numbers are in conflict.
Clean claim rate predicts the other metrics 30 to 60 days in advance. A clean claim rate that drops in January will show up as elevated Days in AR in February and elevated denial rate in March.
Medicare typically pays within 14 days of a clean claim.
correct_statement: Fourteen days is Medicare's floor, not its ceiling. A clean electronic claim cannot be paid before the 14th day after receipt (paper: 29th day) and must be paid within 30 days, after which interest accrues (4.75% for July-December 2026). Physician Medicare fee-for-service claims averaged 18.9 days to payment in 2015 remittance data.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Ch. 1, ss. 80.2.1.1-80.2.1.2 (Rev. 13725, issued 04-10-26); First Coast Service Options FAQ on the payment floor; 42 CFR 405.922; Treasury prompt payment rate (July-Dec. 2026); Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325
practice_impact: Medicare Part B is the core payer: expect electronic First Coast payments from day 14, treat any clean claim unpaid at day 30 as an exception with interest due, and avoid paper claims (29-day floor).

claim: Some Medicare Advantage plans take 30 to 45 days [to pay a clean claim].
correct_statement: Some Medicare Advantage claims do take 30-45 days, but no rule entitles plans to it. Plans must pay 95% of non-contract clean claims within 30 days, with interest after; contracted claims follow the contract's prompt-pay clause. UnitedHealthcare says most claims adjudicate within 15 days, up to 45. In 2015 data MA averaged 14.3 days.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Strategic improvements in your RCM to reduce your practice's claim denials' (Mar. 6, 2024); 42 CFR 422.520 and 422.402 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide; Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325; S. 2879/H.R. 5454 bill status (still in committee as of Sept. 2026 data)
practice_impact: MA covers a large share of Florida seniors: read each MA contract's prompt-pay clause, pursue non-contract clean claims unpaid at day 30 (interest is owed) and do not accept 45 days as a given; state prompt-pay law is generally preempted for MA.

claim: Some Medicaid programs take 60 or more [days]; these are structural delays that cannot be fixed by the practice.
correct_statement: Medicaid is the slowest payer class (2015 means: 39 days fee-for-service, 27 managed care, 19 Medicare), but 60-plus days breaches the standard. Federal rules require 90% of clean practitioner claims paid within 30 days and 99% within 90; Florida Medicaid plans must pay, deny or contest electronic claims within 20 days, with 12% interest on overdue payments.
source_title: 42 CFR 447.45 and 447.46 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 409.967(2)(j) and 641.3155 (2026 Florida Statutes); Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, 'The Complexity of Billing and Paying for Physician Care', Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325 (author manuscript on bea.gov)
practice_impact: Dual-eligible crossover claims are this practice's Medicaid exposure (Medicaid as secondary payer averaged 51.8 days in the same study); age them separately and escalate Florida Medicaid plan claims past 20 days, since unpaid claims become an uncontestable obligation at 120 days.

claim: Aged AR that is not resolved within 90 to 120 days of service typically becomes uncollectable (filing window closed, appeal deadline passed, or account sent to collections).
correct_statement: There is no general 90-120-day cliff. Medicare allows one calendar year from service to file and 120 days from the denial notice to request redetermination; Florida-regulated insurers and HMOs have a 6-month filing period; Medicaid fee-for-service allows 12 months. The short clocks are 90-day contract filing limits, Florida's 90-day secondary-claim deadline and MA non-contract 60-day appeals.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44, 405.942, 447.45(d)(1), 422.582 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(3)(b) and 641.3155(2)(b) (2026 Florida Statutes); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide and MA non-contracted provider dispute notice
practice_impact: For a Medicare-heavy practice, treating AR as dead at 90-120 days would abandon collectible money; key each account to its payer's actual clock, counted from the denial notice, and send secondary claims within 90 days of Medicare's determination (the Florida statutory and common contract limit).

claim: Any denial past the appeal window is not workable - it should be written off and documented as a process failure.
correct_statement: A missed appeal window does not end a Medicare claim. The contractor may accept a late redetermination request for good cause, and a party may request a (discretionary) reopening within 1 year of the initial determination for any reason, within 4 years for good cause, or at any time to correct a clerical error. MA reconsiderations also allow good-cause extensions.
source_title: 42 CFR 405.942(b), 405.980(c), 405.986, 422.582(c) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 34 (Reopening and Revision of Claim Determinations and Decisions); Fla. Stat. 408.7057(2)(d) (2026)
practice_impact: Before writing off a First Coast denial older than 120 days, test it for a clerical-error reopening, a one-year reopening or a good-cause late appeal; the vendor's rule would discard recoverable Medicare money.

claim: Every claim that fails on first submission adds 20 to 45 days to its AR age.
correct_statement: No published source gives a 20-45 day penalty per failed claim; none was found in MGMA, HFMA, AAPC or peer-reviewed literature. Delay depends on failure type and correction speed: front-end rejections return on 999/277CA acknowledgment reports (Florida plans must acknowledge e-claims within 24 hours after the next business day begins), and Medicare restarts its 14-day payment floor on resubmission.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, s. 80.2.1 (Rev. 13725, issued 04-10-26); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(4)(a) (2026 Florida Statutes)
practice_impact: Measure the practice's own rejection-to-resubmission lag from clearinghouse and 277CA reports rather than assuming 20-45 days; for Medicare the unavoidable cost of a rejection is a fresh 14-day floor.

claim: Raising clean claim rate from 87 to 94 percent 'will see days in AR drop by 5 to 8 days within 60 days without any other intervention'.
correct_statement: No published source supports a 5-8 day drop, and the vendor's own inputs give far less. Moving 7 percentage points of claims from a 45-60 day cycle to 14-21 days saves 24-46 days on 7% of claims, about 1.7-3.2 days of average AR. A 5-8 day drop would need each fixed claim to save 71-114 days.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; calculation from the vendor's own figures (KPI 03, Section 3); HFMA MAP Keys, 2023 edition (metric definitions only)
practice_impact: Do not forecast a 5-8 day AR improvement from clean-claim work alone; the vendor's own numbers support about 2-3 days.

claim: A contract paying 5 percent above market rate on a 45-day cycle 'may generate less actual cash per quarter' than one paying market rate on a 21-day cycle.
correct_statement: In steady state, cash per quarter follows the rate, not the lag: the 5%-higher contract pays 5% more every quarter. A 24-day slower cycle lowers cash only in the first quarter (cumulative cash catches up in about 17 months) and costs about 0.5% of revenue a year to finance at the 7% prime rate.
source_title: Arithmetic check; Federal Reserve H.15 Selected Interest Rates (release of Nov. 9, 2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026 Florida Statutes); 42 CFR 422.520(b)
practice_impact: Do not trade fee-schedule rate for faster payment on this logic: a 5% rate premium is worth roughly ten times the carrying cost of 24 days. Seek prompt-pay terms in MA contracts as an addition, not a swap.

claim: For most commercial payers, the appeal deadline is 90 to 180 days from service date.
correct_statement: Commercial appeal deadlines run from the remittance or denial date, not the service date, and are mostly longer: UnitedHealthcare 12 months from the original EOB/PRA; Aetna and Cigna 180 calendar days from the initial decision; Florida Blue one year from the remittance advice. ERISA gives claimants at least 180 days after the denial notice.
source_title: UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide (effective Apr. 1, 2026); Aetna 'Disputes and appeals overview' and Cigna 'Appeals and Disputes' (read Nov. 10, 2026); Florida Blue, 'Provider Appeal Changes' (June 2025); 29 CFR 2560.503-1(h)(3)(i); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(19)
practice_impact: Commercial and employer-plan claims are a small share here, but dating appeals from the service date (with the vendor's write-off rule) would wrongly retire appealable claims; load each payer's clock from the remittance date.

claim: Clean claims submitted to most payers will pay or deny within 14 to 30 days.
correct_statement: Broadly right for electronic clean claims. Medicare pays between day 14 and day 30; Florida-regulated insurers, HMOs and Medicaid plans must pay, deny or contest within 20 days (40 for paper); ERISA plans must decide post-service claims within 30 days. Mean time to payment in 2015 data: private 13.7 days, MA 14.3, Medicare 18.9, Medicaid 26.5-39.2.
source_title: Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026 Florida Statutes); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 1, s. 80.2.1 (Rev. 13725); 29 CFR 2560.503-1(f)(2)(iii)(B); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide; Gottlieb, Shapiro & Dunn, Health Affairs 2018;37(4):619-626, doi:10.1377/hlthaff.2017.1325
practice_impact: Usable rule of thumb: an electronic claim with no payment or denial by day 30 (day 20 for Florida-regulated plans) needs a status check rather than more waiting.

claim: Payers with 365-day timely filing windows have claims that are genuinely recoverable at 150 or 180 days.
correct_statement: Correct for filing: Medicare allows one calendar year from the date of service, Medicaid fee-for-service 12 months, and UnitedHealthcare says MA plans must give non-contract providers 365 days, so an unfiled or rejected claim is still billable at day 150-180. A denied Medicare claim instead needs redetermination within 120 days of the notice, or a reopening.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.44(a)(1), 447.45(d)(1), 405.942, 405.980 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide
practice_impact: Medicare fee-for-service claims, the core of a geriatrics payer mix, stay fileable for a year, so aged Medicare AR deserves a worked queue; check the 120-day appeal clock on denied claims, and note secondary claims to Florida-regulated plans are due 90 days after the primary's determination.

claim: For 0-30 day claims, verification that the claim was received and is in process 'can be batch-checked via ERA rather than individually worked'.
correct_statement: An ERA (X12 835) reports only finalized claims, so it cannot confirm that a pending claim was received. Receipt is confirmed by the 999 and 277CA acknowledgment reports; in-process status comes from the 276/277 claim status transaction or the payer portal, which can be run in batch. Claims rejected at the front end never produce an ERA.
source_title: CMS, 'Health Care Payment and Remittance Advice' and 'Claim Status Request and Response' (pages last modified 09/10/2024); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 24, s. 50.3.1 (Rev. 13954, issued 09-29-26); 45 CFR 162.1401-162.1402 and 162.1601-162.1602
practice_impact: A claim rejected at the front end never appears on an ERA; if 0-30 day claims are 'verified' by ERA, rejections sit unseen until they age. Reconcile every batch against 999/277CA reports daily.

claim: Historical recovery rate for the 120-plus day bucket is 'typically 30 to 50 percent for most independent practices'.
correct_statement: No published benchmark gives a 30-50% recovery rate for AR older than 120 days. The only figures found are unsourced: Physicians Practice says about 10 cents on the dollar past 120 days, and MGMA cites 10-20% for collection-agency recoveries. The vendor's own KPI 03 says AR unresolved at 90-120 days 'typically becomes uncollectable'. Use the practice's own recovery history.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; MGMA, 'A structured approach to collecting patient A/R' (Dec. 7, 2022); Physicians Practice, 'Claim denials, patient collections and the revenue cycle' (Mar. 6, 2026)
practice_impact: This rate drives the vendor's write-off forecast; replace it with the practice's own 12-month recovery rate for the 120-plus bucket, by payer.

claim: Most practices use $100 minimum for collections referral.
correct_statement: No survey reports the dollar minimum practices use for collections referral. MGMA's poll covers timing only (42% refer at 91-120 days, 32% after 120, 10% never). Examples vary widely: MGMA advises in-house calls only above $100, and a Physicians Practice Q&A describes an agency refusing accounts under $500. Credit bureaus removed medical collections under $500 in 2023.
source_title: No traceable source for the statistic; MGMA, 'A structured approach to collecting patient A/R' (Dec. 7, 2022); CFPB, 'Have medical debt? Anything already paid or under $500 should no longer be on your credit report' (May 8, 2023, archived page)
practice_impact: Little: set the threshold from the agency contract. The real exposure is referring Medicare cost-sharing of QMB dual eligibles, which federal law forbids billing at all.

claim: When an account is referred to collections or written off, 'the documented contact history is the compliance record that demonstrates due diligence'.
correct_statement: A contact log helps but is not 'the compliance record'. OIG expects a good-faith effort to collect Medicare cost-sharing; write-offs need documented financial need or reasonable collection efforts and must not be routine. QMB patients cannot be billed Medicare cost-sharing at all, and Florida bars patient collection while a contested claim is pending. Medicare bad-debt documentation rules exclude fee-schedule services.
source_title: 42 CFR 1003.110 ('Remuneration') and 413.89(i)(1) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); OIG Special Fraud Alert, 59 FR 65372 (Dec. 19, 1994); CMS Qualified Medicare Beneficiary Program page (modified 03/16/2026); Fla. Stat. 627.6131(9) and 559.72 (2026); IRS Topic 453
practice_impact: Nursing-facility patients are often dual eligibles with QMB protection: screen QMB status before any statement or referral, and keep hardship determinations and a written, uniformly applied write-off policy alongside the contact log.

claim: A new provider whose claims concentrate in the 61-plus day buckets within their first 60 days has a credentialing gap (NPI not active with a payer, wrong taxonomy codes, or fee schedule not loaded).
correct_statement: Enrollment gaps are a common cause, but the test fails as written: aged from date of service, no claim can be 61-plus days old in a provider's first 60 days. For Medicare, billing privileges start on the later of the application filing date or first service date, with 30 days of retrospective billing, so late filing forfeits earlier claims.
source_title: 42 CFR 424.520(d), 424.521(a), 424.522(a) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); HFMA MAP Keys, 2023 edition (AR-1 aging definition)
practice_impact: File each new clinician's PECOS enrollment and reassignment before the first facility visit; Medicare reaches back only 30 days before the filing date, so monitor held-claim counts weekly instead of waiting for a 61-plus bucket.

claim: Research across independent practices consistently shows the probability of collecting a patient balance in full drops from about 95% at time of service to 70-80% after a first statement, 50-60% after a second, and 30-40% in collections.
correct_statement: No study with this curve was found; similar ladders appear only in unsourced vendor blogs that disagree with one another. Measured data differ: practices collected about 90% (2019) and 56% (2022) of copays at time of service, hospital-system datasets show 42-54% of insured patient balances collected, and surveyed medical collection agencies report median recovery near 10-15%, not 30-40%.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Patient balance collection: What's moving the numbers and how to get ahead' (Oct. 22, 2025); CFPB Regulation V final rule preamble, 90 FR 3276, 3320-3324 (Jan. 14, 2025); Ippolito et al., JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (PubMed PMID 40779258); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026)
practice_impact: Do not model cash on this curve: nursing-facility Part B coinsurance is billed after adjudication, mostly to Medigap or Medicaid, so the 95% time-of-service tier does not exist here.

claim: A copay collection rate below 95% means the front desk is not collecting money the practice has an absolute right to collect at every visit.
correct_statement: There is no absolute right. Federal law bars every Medicare provider, including in Medicare Advantage, from collecting Medicare deductibles, coinsurance or copays from QMBs. Florida Medicaid exempts institutional residents from copays and Medicaid payment is payment in full. Original Medicare Part B carries 20% coinsurance, not visit copays, and First Coast recommends not collecting it before Medicare pays.
source_title: CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN7936176, Prohibition on Billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries (Sept. 2025); CMS QMB Program page (modified 03/16/2026); 42 U.S.C. 1396a(n)(3)(B); 42 CFR 422.504(g)(1)(iii); Fla. Stat. 409.9081, 409.907(3)(j) (2026); First Coast, 'When not to show patient paid amounts on claims' (Oct. 29, 2024)
practice_impact: Dual-eligible/QMB facility residents cannot be charged Medicare cost sharing; knowingly billing duals outside assignment carries penalties up to $19,940 per violation (45 CFR 102.3) plus refunds, so a 95% copay KPI is the wrong yardstick.

claim: A POS collection rate above 90% is best practice, is achievable, and should be the target for every independent practice.
correct_statement: No MGMA or HFMA benchmark was found that sets 90% for a blended point-of-service rate. MGMA data show practices collected about 90% of copays at time of service in 2019 but 56% in 2022, and only 15%-39% of patient-due balances. Kodiak's standard metric, POS cash as a share of patient payments, has a median near 16%. Not a universal target.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Patient balance collection: What's moving the numbers and how to get ahead' (Oct. 22, 2025); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); HFMA, 'Patient POS collections pose a growing problem for RCM departments' (June 8, 2026)
practice_impact: Facility visits have no check-in desk and Medicare coinsurance is unknown until adjudication, so a 90% POS target is inapplicable; measure post-adjudication patient and secondary collection instead.

claim: A $200 balance sent through two statements and a collections referral yields $60 to $80 gross; after a typical 25 to 40 percent agency fee the net recovery is $36 to $60.
correct_statement: The arithmetic is right and 25-40% contingency fees match trade reports, but a 30-40% gross recovery is well above documented medical collection results: an ACA International member survey found median rates of 14.5% in 2022 falling to 9.6% in late 2023, and CFPB put the baseline below 25%. A $200 referral more plausibly nets about $12-$37.
source_title: CFPB, Prohibition on Creditors and Consumer Reporting Agencies Concerning Medical Information (Regulation V), final rule preamble, 90 FR 3276, 3320 and 3324 (Jan. 14, 2025; rule vacated July 2025); AAPC Practice Management Alert, 'Six Tips for Hiring a Collection Agency' (Sept. 2001)
practice_impact: Budget on roughly 10-20% gross agency recovery, not 30-40%; QMB and Medicaid-covered coinsurance can never be placed with an agency.

claim: Every patient with a known balance (copay, prior balance, or estimated deductible) is told the amount and asked for payment before they are roomed.
correct_statement: Not lawful or advisable for every patient. QMBs may not be asked to pay Medicare cost sharing; providers generally may not deny Medicaid services over an unpaid copay, and institutional residents owe none. For Original Medicare, First Coast recommends collecting no deductible or coinsurance until Part B pays, because over-collection is program abuse. The rule fits commercial copays only.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, 'When not to show patient paid amounts on claims' (Oct. 29, 2024); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 1 §30.3.1.1 and §30.3.3 (chapter as of Rev. 13725, 04-10-26); CMS MLN7936176 (Sept. 2025); 42 CFR 447.52(e), 447.56(a)(1)(viii); Fla. Stat. 409.9081(3)(c) (2026)
practice_impact: Nursing-facility and ALF visits have no check-in or rooming step; bill coinsurance after the Medicare remittance, report any pre-collected amount on the claim, and screen every account for QMB/Medicaid status first.

claim: For balances above $200 the front desk immediately offers a payment plan, such as $50 per month, with automated monthly charges to the card on file.
correct_statement: Payment plans are lawful, but conditions are missing. A written agreement payable in more than four installments (any balance above $200 at $50 a month) makes a practice that does this more than 25 times a year a Regulation Z creditor owing Truth in Lending disclosures. Recurring debit-card or bank-account charges need signed written authorization under Regulation E.
source_title: 12 CFR 1026.2(a)(14), (a)(17) and Supplement I comment 2(a)(17)(i)-1 (Regulation Z); 12 CFR 1005.10(b), (d) (Regulation E); eCFR current as of Nov. 6, 2026
practice_impact: Point-of-visit plans rarely arise in facility-based care, but any written plan program needs TILA-compliant forms and signed card authorizations, and must exclude QMB/dual-eligible cost sharing, which cannot be billed.

claim: Collectible means the patient is not on a payment plan, financial assistance program, or hardship waiver that legitimately defers collection; a written charity care policy with income thresholds lets the practice keep a firm standard.
correct_statement: OIG permits waiving Medicare cost sharing for financial need only if the waiver is not routine, not advertised, and follows a good-faith individualized assessment under uniform, documented, objective guidelines. The definition also omits balances uncollectible by law (QMB cost sharing, Medicaid payment-in-full), and Florida treats a general business practice of waiving insureds' copays or deductibles as insurance fraud.
source_title: 42 CFR 1003.110 (definition of 'Remuneration'); OIG Supplemental Compliance Program Guidance for Hospitals, 70 FR 4858, 4871 (Jan. 31, 2005); OIG Special Fraud Alert on routine waiver of copayments, 59 FR 65372 (Dec. 19, 1994); Fla. Stat. 817.234(7)(a) (2026)
practice_impact: Use a written hardship policy with documented per-patient determinations, never advertise it, and code QMB/Medicaid adjustments separately from hardship write-offs; beneficiary-inducement penalties reach $25,595 per item or service.

claim: Without active management, most practices' POS collection rate settles between 60 and 70 percent, and a team trained to 90 percent can fall to 65 percent within 60 days of one experienced staff departure.
correct_statement: No survey or study was found for a 60-70% resting rate or for a drop from 90% to 65% within 60 days of one departure; both appear to be vendor assertions. MGMA benchmarking shows time-of-service copay collection of about 90% in 2019 and 56% in 2022, a different measure that says nothing about turnover effects.
source_title: MGMA Stat, 'Patient balance collection: What's moving the numbers and how to get ahead' (Oct. 22, 2025)
practice_impact: little (a facility-based practice has no front-desk point-of-service collection)

claim: In many independent practices, patient responsibility now represents 20 to 35 percent of total revenue.
correct_statement: Only the low end has support, and as a share of allowed amounts for insured patients: AMA's 2013 report card found nearly one-quarter and Kodiak about 23% in early 2026. Nationally, out-of-pocket payments were 8.5% of physician and clinical services spending in 2024; Kodiak put insured patient responsibility at 7.3% of net revenue for 2025. Nothing supports 35%.
source_title: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, Table 8 (2024 data) and NHE Fact Sheet (modified 06/24/2026); Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Reports (Mar. and June 2026); Medical Economics on AMA National Health Insurer Report Card (July 10, 2013); KFF, 'A Snapshot of Sources of Coverage Among Medicare Beneficiaries' (Dec. 19, 2025)
practice_impact: For a Medicare/Medicaid nursing-facility panel the patient-paid share should be far below 20%: coinsurance goes to Medigap or Medicaid crossover, and Florida Medicaid often pays $0 on dual-eligible coinsurance (s. 409.908(13)(b)) that cannot be billed to the patient.

claim: Research consistently shows statements received within 30 days of service produce payment rates 25 to 35 percentage points higher than those received after 60 days.
correct_statement: No study quantifying a 25-35 point payment-rate gap between statements received within 30 days and after 60 days was found; similar figures appear only in unsourced vendor material. Measured data address bill size and elapsed time generally: across 1,348 practices, 93.8% of small balances but 66.7% of balances over $200 were collected within 12 months.
source_title: Chernew M, Bush J, 'As Patients Take On More Costs, Will Providers Shoulder The Burden?', Health Affairs Forefront (May 4, 2017), as quoted by PNHP (original page returned HTTP 403)
practice_impact: Send statements promptly after the Medicare remittance, but do not expect a proven 25-35 point lift; most balances here belong to secondary payers rather than patients.

claim: Every dollar that passes through the statement cycle costs $8 to $15 to collect and recovers at a fraction of face value.
correct_statement: As written it is a unit error: a dollar cannot cost $8-$15 to collect. The vendor's own Front-End RCM Playbook says $8-$14 per statement, and no MGMA, HFMA or CAQH source was found for that either. Published statement-mailing fees run about $1 per statement (Elation Billing charges $0.95) before staff time.
source_title: Elation Health Help Center, 'What are the delivery charges for sending patient statements in Elation Billing' (accessed Nov. 10, 2026); 2025 CAQH Index Executive Report; vendor Front-End RCM Playbook (internal inconsistency)
practice_impact: Compute the practice's own cost per statement (vendor fee, postage, staff minutes); do not carry $8-$15 into cost-to-collect models.

claim: The collections agency recovers 20 to 35 cents on the dollar on average; recovery rates below 20 percent should prompt consideration of a different agency.
correct_statement: Overstated. The best public data put medical collection agency recovery well below this: an ACA International member survey showed median rates of 14.5% in 2022 falling to 9.6% in late 2023, and CFPB concluded the baseline is under 25%. Older trade sources cite 15-19% averages. A 20% floor would flag typical agency performance, not poor performance.
source_title: CFPB, Prohibition on Creditors and Consumer Reporting Agencies Concerning Medical Information (Regulation V), final rule preamble, 90 FR 3276, 3320 and 3324 (Jan. 14, 2025; rule vacated July 2025); AAPC Practice Management Alert, 'Six Tips for Hiring a Collection Agency' (Sept. 2001); Physicians Practice Q&A (June 2004)
practice_impact: Expect roughly 10-20 cents on the dollar gross, less a 25-40% fee, on the few truly patient-owed balances; never refer QMB or Medicaid-covered balances, and confirm the agency is registered in Florida (s. 559.553).

claim: Every account that meets the referral criteria (minimum balance, days from service, completed statement series, no active payment plan) is referred to collections without exception.
correct_statement: Law requires exceptions the listed criteria omit. QMB cost-sharing balances may never be billed or sent to collections; Florida Medicaid payment is payment in full; HMO subscribers cannot be pursued for amounts the HMO owes; bills in federal patient-provider dispute resolution cannot go to collections; and bankruptcy stays collection. Uniform policy is sound only after these screens.
practice_impact: A no-exceptions rule would send dual-eligible/QMB coinsurance to an agency, a federal violation; add QMB, Medicaid, HMO-liability, dispute and bankruptcy holds to the referral checklist before any account is released.

claim: A patient collection rate above 90% is best practice and is still achievable in a high-deductible environment; below 60% is structural failure.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or AAPC benchmark with these tiers was found. Measured results are lower: across 1,348 practices, 93.8% of balances of $35 or less but only 66.7% of balances over $200 were collected within 12 months (2015), and Kodiak reports insured patients paid 42.4% of what they owed in 2025. Above 90% is documented only for small, copay-size balances.
source_title: Kodiak Solutions KPI Benchmarking Report (Mar. 2026); Chernew and Bush, Health Affairs Forefront (May 4, 2017), as quoted by PNHP; Ippolito et al., JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (PubMed PMID 40779258, doi:10.1001/jamahealthforum.2025.2284)
practice_impact: Benchmark only truly patient-owed balances after excluding QMB, Medicaid and secondary-payer amounts; otherwise legally required write-offs will make the practice look like a 'structural failure'.

claim: A written payment plan policy sets minimum payment, maximum duration and whether interest is charged; most practices charge no interest for plans under 12 months, with automatic monthly charges to a card on file.
correct_statement: A written policy is sound, but conditions are missing. A written plan payable in more than four installments (even at 0%), or any plan with interest, makes a practice doing this more than 25 times a year a Regulation Z creditor owing Truth in Lending disclosures. Florida caps interest at 18% simple. No data support 'most practices charge no interest.'
source_title: 12 CFR 1026.2(a)(17) and Official Interpretation comment 2(a)(17)(i)-1 (Regulation Z, CFPB); 12 CFR 1005.10(b) (Regulation E); Fla. Stat. 687.02(1) (2026)
practice_impact: If more than 25 written plans a year are signed, give closed-end TILA disclosures and keep signed card authorizations; apply plans only to balances patients legally owe, never QMB or Medicaid cost sharing.

claim: ERA enrollment is free and is the single most impactful administrative change most practices have not completed.
correct_statement: Payer ERA enrollment generally carries no charge: Medicare's is free with free CMS viewing software, and plans must send standard ERAs on request. But clearinghouses and payment vendors often charge fees, and ERA is already the norm: CAQH's 2025 Index shows 87% of medical-plan remittance advice fully electronic. 'Single most impactful' is unsupported.
source_title: 2025 CAQH Index Executive Report; Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 24 §40.2.4.4 (chapter as of Rev. 13954, 09-29-26); First Coast, 'Electronic remittance advice -- what you need to know' (Aug. 11, 2026); 45 CFR 162.925(a); CMS Guidance Letter GL-2022-04 (Mar. 22, 2022); AMA, 'Physicians protected from health plan credit card fees'
practice_impact: Confirm 835 enrollment with First Coast, each Medicare Advantage plan and Florida Medicaid, and check what the clearinghouse charges per ERA; this is routine hygiene, not a breakthrough.

claim: For write-offs coded 'denial appeal expired' or 'timely filing', the quarterly recovery review asks: 'Is there a balance transfer to patient responsibility that was never executed?'
Rejected claims, claims returned before adjudication, restart their AR clock when resubmitted, but the original service date governs the timely filing deadline.
Every denial that is categorized as appealable must have an appeal filed within 30 days of receipt ... A filed appeal stops the clock on the appeal deadline.
Accounts written off as 'denial appeal expired' may have a secondary recovery path, including 'a small claims or arbitration option for large amounts'.
Any timely filing write-off is a 100% preventable revenue loss, the claim was never denied for clinical or coverage reasons.
Bad debt (uncollected patient): below 3% of net revenue is acceptable; 3% to 5% is a warning zone; above 5% of net revenue is the action threshold.

Timely filing write-offs above 0.5% of gross charges and expired-appeal denial write-offs above 1% of gross charges are action thresholds; preventable write-offs should be less than 5 percent of total write-offs.
The recovery rate from these retrospective reviews is typically 10 to 15 percent of the dollar amount reviewed.
Net Collection Rate = (Payments Received) / (Charges Billed minus Contractual Adjustments).
A 5 percent improvement in clean claim rate typically produces a 1 to 2 percent improvement in net collection rate with a 60-day lag.

Patient responsibility is commonly estimated at roughly 20 to 35 percent of net collectible revenue for most practices ... A patient collection rate of 75 percent means ... a direct 5 to 9 percent drag on net collection rate.
A practice with a net collection rate of 97 percent ... commands a higher valuation multiple than a peer practice at 89 percent with the same clinical volume.

A primary care practice with 45 percent Medicaid volume will have a structurally lower achievable net collection rate ... because Medicaid's lower rates and higher administrative burden create a different collection environment.
The percentage of AR over 120 days is the most predictive leading indicator of net collection rate. [Unworked aged AR] will become write-offs within one to two quarters.
The decomposition in Section 2 will almost always reveal one component that contributes 40 to 60 percent of the total collection gap.
Every payer has a timely filing deadline - typically 90 days, 180 days, or one year from service date, depending on the payer.
some Medicare Advantage plans require submission within 90 days, some commercial payers within 60 days

For any service within 30 days of its timely filing deadline: enter the charge immediately and submit the claim the same day, regardless of documentation completeness; most payers allow medical record submissions to support pending claims.
A claim that misses the timely filing deadline because someone was waiting for a complete note is not recoverable at any documentation quality level.
Same day or next day (0-1 days) is best practice; 1-2 days acceptable; 3-5 days is the action threshold; above 5 days is a significant problem.
A practice with a 4-day average charge lag has every claim starting its AR clock 4 days late. The practice reports 42 days in AR. The effective AR age - from service date to payment - is 46 days.
hospital progress notes completed within 24 hours of the encounter, operative notes completed and dictated within 24 hours of the procedure, discharge summaries completed within 24 hours of discharge

The monthly surgical charge reconciliation shows a discrepancy rate below 2 percent... A reconciliation discrepancy rate above 5 percent means the intraoperative charge capture workflow is not functioning consistently.
Collections agency commissions: variable by contract terms, typically around 1 percent of collections referred.
Industry benchmarks for claims per FTE per month range from 750 to 1,200 for outpatient practices depending on complexity.

A rejected claim that must be corrected and resubmitted costs approximately three to five times as much in billing staff time as a clean claim... A denied claim that requires an appeal costs five to ten times as much.

Staff cost (salaries + benefits + management overhead): typically 70 to 80 percent of total billing cost in in-house operations... Technology cost (PMS, clearinghouse, eligibility tools, patient portal): typically 10 to 15 percent.

Establish a small balance write-off threshold... balances below the threshold [$25 or $50] receive one automated statement and are written off if not paid within 30 days, without any manual follow-up.
In a well-managed billing operation, rework activities should consume no more than 25 to 30 percent of total billing staff time.

Cost to collect should include all direct and allocated costs of the revenue cycle function: billing staff salaries and benefits, management overhead, clearinghouse fees, statement costs, practice management system fees, collections agency commissions, and outsourced billing fees.
Many practices that outsource billing do so at a higher cost to collect than their internal operation
Our coders and providers are current on the 2021 E&M guideline changes and correctly apply the medical decision-making pathway.
correct_statement: The 2021 revisions covered only office and outpatient visits (99202-99215). Since January 1, 2023 nursing facility, home or residence and hospital visits are also leveled by medical decision making or total time; history and exam no longer set the level. Later changes include G2211 for home visits (2026) and its replacement by modifier B1 on January 1, 2027.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, 'Nursing facility E/M services' (June 26, 2026); CMS MLN Booklet MLN006764, Evaluation and Management Services (May 2026); AMA, CPT E/M Code and Guideline Changes effective January 1, 2023, and CPT Evaluation and Management page; CMS fact sheet, CY 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (Nov. 4, 2026; 91 FR 70992, Nov. 9, 2026)
practice_impact: Nearly all facility-practice visits use nursing facility (99304-99310) and home or residence (99341-99350) codes the 2021 rules never covered; staff current only to 2021 miss the 2023 rules, prolonged codes G0317/G0318 and the January 2027 modifier B1 change.

claim: Copays are collected at check-in, before the patient is roomed, at every visit, with no exceptions.
correct_statement: Exceptions are required by law. Providers may not collect Medicare deductibles, coinsurance or copays from Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries, in Original Medicare or Medicare Advantage. Florida Medicaid exempts institutional residents and managed-care enrollees from copays. Medicare pays annual wellness visits at 100%. First Coast recommends not collecting Part B deductible or coinsurance until Medicare has paid.
source_title: CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN7936176, Prohibition on Billing Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries (Sept. 2025); 42 CFR 422.504(g)(1)(iii), 447.56(a)(1)(viii)-(ix), 447.52(e), 410.152(l) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Fla. Stat. 409.9081(3) and 409.907(3)(j) (2026); First Coast, 'When not to show patient paid amounts on claims' (Oct. 29, 2024); Medicare Claims Processing Manual, Ch. 2, s. 10.4
practice_impact: Facility rounds have no check-in desk, Original Medicare carries coinsurance rather than copays, and QMB or institutional Medicaid residents cannot be charged at all; a no-exceptions rule would produce prohibited collections, refunds and possible sanctions.

claim: Patient responsibility now represents 25 to 35 percent of revenue in most independent practices, and that percentage is growing as high-deductible plans continue to dominate the market.
correct_statement: No source supports 25-35%. CMS national accounts show patients paid 8.5% of physician and clinical spending out of pocket in 2024, unchanged since 2022. The highest measure found, Kodiak's hospital-system data, is about 23% of allowed amounts in first-quarter 2026, flat from 2025, with roughly 30% collected. PPOs cover 50% of covered workers; HSA-qualified high-deductible plans 29%.
source_title: CMS National Health Expenditure Accounts, Table 8, Physician and Clinical Services Expenditures by Source of Funds (2024 data; page updated Jan. 14, 2026); Kodiak Solutions, 'Untangling the patient financial responsibility web' (June 2026) and 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026); KFF 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey (Oct. 22, 2026)
practice_impact: Inapplicable to a Medicare facility practice: high-deductible plans are irrelevant, cost sharing is the 20% Part B coinsurance, billed first to any Medigap or Medicaid secondary coverage, and QMB balances cannot be collected; secondary and crossover billing matters more than patient pay.

claim: Total score 31, 46 (AT RISK): 'Likely costing $50,000, $150,000 annually in preventable revenue loss.' Total score 47, 61 (MODERATE): 'Likely $20K, $50K recoverable annually.'
correct_statement: No study, survey or published method links this vendor's 77-point yes/no self-assessment to dollar losses, and the guide gives none. The bands are fixed amounts that ignore practice size. Measured leakage is reported as rates, not flat dollars: Kodiak's 2025 medians were a 2.7% final denial rate and a 1.3% bad debt rate.
source_title: No source found for the claim. Comparator: Kodiak Solutions, 'State of the healthcare revenue cycle' (Mar. 2026). Vendor text checked: Scoring Interpretation Guide (pp. 7-8) and Overall Practice Rating (pp. 36-37)
practice_impact: Do not budget or justify purchases from these dollar bands; size any opportunity from the practice's own denial, write-off and underpayment data as a percentage of its revenue.

claim: Our overall patient collection rate is at or above 90% of patient responsibility billed.
correct_statement: No MGMA or HFMA benchmark setting 90% for overall patient collections was found. Measured rates are far lower: across 1,348 practices, 93.8% of balances of $35 or less but 66.7% of balances over $200 were paid within a year (2015); insured patients paid 42.4% of what they owed in 2025; hospital-system yield was about 30% in early 2026.
source_title: Ippolito B, Trish E, Duffy EL, Vabson B, 'Patient Repayment of US Hospital Bills From 2018 to 2024', JAMA Health Forum 2025;6(8):e252284 (PubMed PMID 40779258, doi:10.1001/jamahealthforum.2025.2284); Chernew M, Bush J, Health Affairs Blog (May 4, 2017), as reproduced by PNHP; Kodiak Solutions reports (Mar. and June 2026); MGMA Stat (Oct. 22, 2025); HFMA MAP Keys (2026)
practice_impact: QMB and Medicaid balances are uncollectible by law and must leave the denominator; track secondary and crossover payments and non-QMB coinsurance separately, and do not treat a rate under 90% on larger balances as failure.

claim: We offer structured payment plans with automatic payment required, not open-ended 'send us what you can' arrangements.
correct_statement: Written payment plans are lawful, but mandatory autopay carries conditions the guide omits. Federal law bars conditioning credit on repayment by preauthorized electronic fund transfers, so a non-debit option should exist. Recurring bank or debit-card charges need signed authorization with a copy to the patient. Written plans over four installments can trigger Truth in Lending disclosures.
source_title: Electronic Fund Transfer Act, 15 U.S.C. 1693k; Regulation E, 12 CFR 1005.10(b)-(e) and Supplement I comment 10(e)(1)-1; Regulation Z, 12 CFR 1026.2(a)(17)(i), (v) and comment 2(a)(17)(i)-1 (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026). No agency ruling found applying the compulsory-use ban specifically to interest-free medical payment plans
practice_impact: Residents' bills are often paid by relatives or representatives: get the account holder's own signed authorization, offer a credit-card or non-automatic option, and never place QMB or Medicaid cost sharing on a plan.

claim: Our patient payment portal allows a patient to click a link, see their balance, and complete payment in under two minutes, without requiring a username, password, or portal login.
correct_statement: HIPAA does not prescribe usernames or passwords, but a named patient's balance is protected health information and the Security Rule requires verifying that the person seeking access is the one claimed. A login-free payment link is acceptable only if it still verifies the recipient, for example by date of birth or one-time code. HHS's 2025 multi-factor proposal is not final.
source_title: HIPAA Security Rule, 45 CFR 164.312(a), (d); Privacy Rule, 45 CFR 160.103, 164.510(b), 164.514(h) (eCFR current to Nov. 6, 2026); Unified Agenda 2026, RIN 0945-AA22 (reginfo.gov); FCC rule 47 CFR 64.1200(a)(9)(iv)(D). No OCR guidance found that addresses login-free payment links specifically
practice_impact: Statements for facility residents often go to relatives or representatives; an unverified link can show a resident's balance to the wrong person, and texted billing links fall outside the TCPA health care message exemption, so prior consent is needed.

claim: Our charge lag standard is defined in writing (target: ≤48 hours for office encounters, ≤5 business days for hospital and procedure encounters) and monitored by provider.
correct_statement: No MGMA, HFMA or Medicare rule sets these targets. HFMA's MAP Keys treat charges posted more than 3 days after service as late in any setting, and MGMA's median service-to-claim lag was 3 days (2018 data). A 48-hour office target is consistent; 5 business days for hospital work is looser. Medicare allows one year to file.
source_title: HFMA MAP Keys, Total Charge Lag Days (PB-4) and Late Charges as a Percentage of Total Charges (CL-2) (hfma.org, 2026); MGMA letter to Senate HELP and House Energy and Commerce leaders (Dec. 9, 2019); MGMA Practice Operations Glossary; 42 CFR 424.44(a)(1); CMS MLN006764 (May 2026)
practice_impact: Nursing facility and assisted living rounds are neither 'office' nor 'hospital' encounters; write a standard for them (3 days matches HFMA and MGMA), monitor it by provider, and bill only after the note is complete and signed.

claim: Industry benchmarks from MGMA and HFMA: median days in AR 45, 55 vs top quartile 30, 38; median clean claim rate 85, 90% vs >96%; median initial denial rate 8, 12% vs <5%.

For a practice billing $4 million annually, the difference between median and top-quartile performance on these three metrics 'can represent $200,000 to $400,000 in additional annual collections'; called 'the documented revenue gap.'

Benchmark targets by practice size: small (<3 providers) days in AR 35, 45, clean claim 90, 93%, denial 7, 10%, net collection 94, 96%, AR over 90 days <20%; large (10+) days in AR 40, 52, net collection 96, 98%.
Clean claim rate: the percentage of claims submitted that are accepted by the payer on first pass without rejection, denial, or request for additional information.
Each payer has timely filing limits, and denials based on timely filing are almost never overturned.
CARC (Claim Adjustment Reason Code) and RARC (Remittance Advice Remark Code) on every denial explanation of benefits 'tell you exactly why the claim was denied.'
For 1, 2 providers: 1, 2 billing staff covering all functions, or outsourced. Full outsourcing is often more cost-effective at this size.
A denial that must be appealed costs 25, 45 minutes of staff time and delays payment 30, 60 days; every dollar invested in denial prevention typically returns 3, 5x in avoided denial management cost.
Medicare's deadline is one year from the date of service. Most commercial payers range from 90 to 180 days, and some managed care contracts impose 60-day windows.
correct_statement: Medicare fee-for-service claims must reach the contractor within 1 calendar year after the date of service (Part B: 'From' date); rejected, unprocessable claims do not count as filed. Commercial windows are contractual, commonly 90 to 180 days; Medicare Advantage follows each plan contract. Florida law sets a non-waivable 6-month period for state-regulated insurers and HMOs. 60-day windows were not confirmed.
source_title: eCFR 42 CFR 424.44 (current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 1 s.70 (Rev. 13725); First Coast Service Options timely filing FAQ; Fla. Stat. 627.6131 and 641.3155 (2026); Florida Blue Manual for Physicians and Providers, claims section (Sept. 2026); Cigna 'When to File Your Claims'; UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide
practice_impact: Calendar First Coast claims at 12 months from the 'From' date, but work to each Medicare Advantage contract's own window (the Florida statute does not reach those plans); fix rejected claims at once because First Coast does not count them as filed.

claim: Payers may deny for late filing and, 'absent a documented administrative error exception, those denials are final'; 'A timely filing denial is not an appeals opportunity. It is a forfeiture.'
correct_statement: Medicare timely-filing denials are not initial determinations and cannot be appealed, but four regulatory exceptions extend the deadline: administrative error, retroactive Medicare entitlement, Medicaid recoupment after retroactive entitlement, and retroactive Medicare Advantage or PACE disenrollment. Commercial and Medicare Advantage timely-filing denials can be reconsidered or appealed with proof of timely submission, so they are not automatically final.
source_title: eCFR 42 CFR 405.926(n) and 424.44(b) (current to Nov. 6, 2026); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 1 s.70.4-70.7 (Rev. 13725); Florida Blue Manual for Physicians and Providers, appeals section (Sept. 2026); UnitedHealthcare 2026 Care Provider Administrative Guide, Ch. 10 'Proof of claim timely filing'; Cigna 'When to File Your Claims'
practice_impact: Do not write these off unread: nursing-home patients often have retroactive Medicare, Medicaid or Medicare Advantage changes that reopen the Medicare window for about six months, and plan denials can be reversed with proof such as an EDI acceptance report.

claim: Review denials for timely filing reason codes - CO-29 on Medicare remits, or equivalent commercial denial codes.
correct_statement: Correct for Part B. First Coast lists 'CO 29' as its timely-filing denial code (Part A uses reject reason code 39011), commonly paired with remark code N211, 'You may not appeal this decision.' Reason code 29 is the national HIPAA code, so commercial and Medicare Advantage electronic remittances carry the same code 29 rather than a different equivalent.
source_title: First Coast Service Options, 'What is the claim timely filing guideline?' (FAQ); X12 Claim Adjustment Reason Codes; Noridian JE Part B 'Timely Filing' reason code guidance (updated Apr. 30, 2025); Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 22 s.60.1; 45 CFR 162.1603
practice_impact: Filter every payer's remittances on reason code 29; the CO group code means a write-off that cannot be billed to the patient, and a rejected claim shows no code 29 until its late resubmission is denied.

claim: HFMA-aligned industry estimate: 1 to 5 percent of collectible revenue is lost to charge capture failure. On $2 million in collections, that is $20,000 to $100,000 per year.
correct_statement: HFMA articles put charge-capture loss at 'as much as 1 percent' of hospital net revenue, based on consultant experience, not a survey. HFMA's 3-5 percent figure covers all hospital revenue leakage, including denials and underpayments, and cites a blog post. No HFMA or MGMA figure for physician practices was found. On $2 million, HFMA's charge-capture figure caps at $20,000.
source_title: HFMA, 'Capturing All Charges: the Operational Reality' (Sept. 20, 2019); HFMA, 'Avoiding the High Cost of High-Capture Leakage' (Aug. 23, 2017); HFMA hfm, 'Why AI is such a promising tool for eliminating a hospital's revenue leakage' (Jan. 30, 2026)
practice_impact: Do not size the opportunity at $20,000-$100,000 per $2 million from this figure; measure the practice's own gap by reconciling facility census and rounding lists to billed charges.

claim: A gastroenterologist performs a colonoscopy with polyp removal - the primary procedure is billed, the polypectomy add-on is missed.
correct_statement: Colonoscopy with polypectomy is not a primary code plus an add-on. It is one stand-alone code (for example 45385, snare removal) that includes and replaces the diagnostic colonoscopy 45378. No colonoscopy code is on CMS's add-on code list. Billing 45378 together with 45385 is unbundling that Medicare's edits deny with no modifier allowed.
source_title: CMS, Medicare NCCI Policy Manual 2026, Ch. VI (rev. 1/1/2026); NCCI Practitioner PTP Edits v323r0 (effective Oct. 1, 2026); CMS Add-on Code Edits file AOC_V2026Q4 (effective Oct. 1, 2026); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D (released Aug. 26, 2026)
practice_impact: Little directly (no endoscopy), but the vendor misdefines add-ons; the real ones here are prolonged-service codes G0317 (nursing facility), G0316 (hospital) and G0318 (home), 99498 (extra advance care planning time) and, since January 1, 2026, G2211 on home or assisted-living visits (not nursing-facility visits).

claim: Office 'injectable medications, diagnostic supplies, or procedure kits' are 'items that have specific HCPCS codes and separate reimbursement'; unbilled supplies and implants are costs 'your payer contracts allow you to recover'.
correct_statement: Only part holds. In the office, Medicare pays separately for physician-purchased injectable drugs and diagnostic imaging agents, but routine supplies, surgical trays and procedure kits are bundled into the procedure payment. In hospitals and nursing facilities the physician generally cannot bill supplies or implants, and drugs and incident-to services for Part A skilled nursing residents belong on the facility's bill.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 s.20.4.2 and 20.4.4 (Rev. 13753); Medicare Benefit Policy Manual Ch. 15 s.50.3 and 60.1 (Rev. 13889); CMS PFS Relative Value File RVU26D; CMS SNF Consolidated Billing page (modified Mar. 3, 2026); UnitedHealthcare Supply Policy, Professional, 2026R0006I
practice_impact: For rounding in hospitals, skilled nursing and nursing facilities there is almost nothing to recover here; supplies and Part A residents' drugs belong on the facility's bill, so billing them risks denials and refunds.

claim: 'For a statistically meaningful sample, pull 25 to 30 encounters per provider being audited', chosen from highest-revenue service types, then 'extrapolate to annual volume to estimate the full-year revenue impact'.
correct_statement: A 25-30 chart review is a reasonable internal probe, in line with OIG's guide of five to ten records per physician and CMS's 20-40-claim probe reviews. It is not statistically valid for extrapolation: validity requires random (probability) selection, not picking the highest-revenue services, and OIG requires at least 100 randomly sampled items to estimate damages in self-disclosures.
source_title: CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual Ch. 8 s.8.4.2 and 8.4.4.3 (Rev. 13762); OIG Compliance Program Guidance for Individual and Small Group Physician Practices, 65 FR 59434 (Oct. 5, 2000); OIG Health Care Fraud Self-Disclosure Protocol (updated Oct. 15, 2026; copy downloaded earlier this session, live re-fetch failed); CMS Targeted Probe and Educate page; 42 CFR 401.305
practice_impact: Fine as a monthly screen, but treat the extrapolated dollar figure as a rough guess; if the review instead finds overbilling, the 60-day report-and-refund rule applies and any sampling must be statistically valid.

claim: The charge master 'should be reviewed at minimum annually' to confirm 'All CPT and HCPCS codes are current - codes are added, deleted, and revised annually'.
correct_statement: Annual review matches only the CPT cycle. The AMA republishes CPT each year, but CMS updates HCPCS Level II codes quarterly (January, April, July, October), the AMA releases Category III codes three times a year and laboratory PLA codes quarterly, and Medicare's add-on code and correct-coding edit files also change quarterly. A charge master with HCPCS codes needs quarterly checks.
source_title: CMS, HCPCS Quarterly Update (modified Sept. 23, 2026) and HCPCS general information; AMA, Category III Codes and CPT PLA Codes pages (updated Oct. 2026); Florida Blue Manual for Physicians and Providers, claims section (Sept. 2026); CMS, Medicare NCCI Procedure to Procedure Edits page
practice_impact: Small: this practice bills few drug or supply codes, but load each January's visit and G-code changes on time and scan the quarterly HCPCS and coding-edit updates.

claim: E&M MDM Score Key: 0, 2 pts = Level 2 | 3, 4 pts = Level 3 | 5, 7 pts = Level 4 | 8, 9 pts = Level 5.

Rubric criteria: Risk 'Low (prescription drug management, minor surgery with identified risk)'; Data 'Extensive (independent interpretation of results OR discussion of management with external provider)'; Problems 'High (... new problem with uncertain prognosis ...)'.
Listed as an undercoding pattern: 'Failing to capture the complexity of prescription drug management, particularly controlled substances, as a high-risk MDM element.'
'New patient codes require higher MDM thresholds but are consistently coded at lower levels out of unfamiliarity.'

'OIG's own published guidance for physician practices suggests a 5, 10 record minimum per payer'; a sample of 25-30 records is said to give 'a stronger statistical base' for a comprehensive internal audit.
False Claims Act (31 U.S.C. §§ 3729-3733) imposes civil liability of up to three times the amount of the false claim plus penalties per claim; 'knowingly' includes reckless disregard.
OIG's Self-Disclosure Protocol 'provides a mechanism for practices to voluntarily report and repay overpayments, typically at a reduced multiplier' compared with a government-initiated investigation.

Medicare requires submission within one year of the date of service; Medicare Part B redetermination: 120 days from date of denial; reconsideration (Level 2): 180 days from date of redetermination decision; QIC reconsideration 'takes 60 days to resolve.'
correct_statement: Part B claims must be filed within 1 calendar year after the date of service. Redetermination: 120 calendar days from receipt of the initial determination notice (receipt presumed 5 days after the notice date). Reconsideration: 180 calendar days from receipt of the redetermination notice. The QIC decides within 60 calendar days, extended up to 14 days per later evidence submission.
source_title: eCFR: 42 CFR 424.44, 405.942, 405.962, 405.970 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'New provider roadmap: Appeals' (Oct. 20, 2025)
practice_impact: Safe to calendar as written (the vendor's wording is about 5 days conservative); but ignore the playbook's nearby line that the one-year limit still runs during an appeal, and note Medicare untimely-filing denials are not appealable (Claims Processing Manual ch. 1, sec. 70.4).

claim: A Medicare Advantage plan 'is required by 42 CFR 422.101 to provide coverage at least as generous as traditional Medicare for all Part A and Part B services'; denying such a claim 'violates that requirement.'
correct_statement: 42 CFR 422.101(a)-(c) requires MA plans to cover all Part A and B services except hospice and kidney acquisition costs, follow NCDs, LCDs and Traditional Medicare coverage rules, and not deny on other criteria. Plans may still require prior authorization, use networks, and apply public internal criteria where Medicare's are not fully established; a denial is not automatically a violation.
practice_impact: A real lever for MA medical-necessity denials if the appeal cites 422.101(b)-(c) plus the specific NCD/LCD; it does not defeat prior-authorization, network or contract denials, and the practice's Part B claims for MA enrollees who have elected hospice go to Original Medicare (First Coast), not the plan.

claim: Medicare Advantage denials: the escalation pathway runs through the MA plan's internal appeal process first, then to an Independent Review Entity designated by CMS, [then] the same multi-level Medicare appeal system that applies to traditional Medicare.
correct_statement: For enrollees and non-contract providers (who must waive enrollee liability), the path is plan reconsideration (request within 60 days), automatic IRE review (C2C since May 1, 2026), then ALJ ($200 threshold in 2026), Appeals Council and federal court ($1,960). A contracted provider's payment denial with no enrollee liability is outside this process; the provider contract's dispute terms govern.
source_title: eCFR: 42 CFR 422.562, 422.582, 422.592, 422.600-422.612 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); CMS, 'Parts C & D Enrollee Grievances, Organization/Coverage Determinations, and Appeals Guidance' (effective July 6, 2026); 90 FR 55869 (2026 amount-in-controversy thresholds)
practice_impact: High: for in-network MA claims the IRE/ALJ ladder is not available to the practice; use each plan's contractual dispute process and deadlines, and reserve the Subpart M route for pre-service requests on the patient's behalf or out-of-network claims with a waiver of liability.

claim: QIC reversal rates for well-supported clinical denials are materially higher than MAC redetermination reversal rates.
correct_statement: CMS data show the opposite in aggregate. For Part B in 2025, 45% of decided MAC redeterminations were fully favorable (3% partially) versus 24% of QIC reconsiderations (1% partially); in 2024 it was 43% versus 20%. Only DME shows a higher QIC rate. CMS publishes no rates for 'well-supported clinical denials,' so that qualifier cannot be tested.
source_title: CMS, 'Original Medicare Claim Appeals Data - 2025' and '- 2024' (Appeals Fact Sheets ZIP on the 'Second Level of Appeal: Reconsideration by a QIC' page, modified Sept. 30, 2026)
practice_impact: Do not expect better odds at the QIC for physician claims; put the full record into the redetermination, and file everything by reconsideration because evidence first offered after the QIC level can be excluded.

claim: The ACA established the right to independent external review for most commercial insurance denials that have exhausted the internal appeal process... IRO decisions are binding on the payer in most states.
correct_statement: The ACA (PHS Act 2719) gives enrollees in non-grandfathered plans external review, but only for denials involving medical judgment, rescissions, or No Surprises Act compliance, not most denials. The IRO decision binds the plan under every compliant state process and under the federal process. Florida has no qualifying state process; its issuers use the HHS-administered or accredited-IRO federal process.
source_title: eCFR: 45 CFR 147.136 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); 42 U.S.C. 300gg-19; CMS/CCIIO external appeals page with state-by-state process list
practice_impact: Little: external review does not reach Medicare, Medicare Advantage or Medicaid; for the few commercial patients it is the patient's request (practice as authorized representative), due within four months, through the federal process rather than a Florida state program.

claim: [MHPAEA] requires that commercial health plans apply the same coverage standards, prior authorization requirements, treatment limitations, and reimbursement rates to [behavioral health] services as they apply to comparable medical and surgical services.
correct_statement: MHPAEA bars financial requirements and treatment limits on mental health/substance use benefits that are more restrictive than the predominant ones applied to substantially all medical/surgical benefits in a classification; prior authorization and rate-setting processes must be comparable and no more stringently applied. It does not require equal reimbursement rates or any behavioral coverage, and does not apply to Medicare.
source_title: eCFR: 45 CFR 146.136 (current as of Nov. 6, 2026); 78 FR 68240 (Nov. 13, 2013) preamble; CMS MHPAEA page (modified Mar. 13, 2026); Departments' statement of non-enforcement of the 2024 rule's new provisions (May 15, 2025)
practice_impact: Little: parity is a commercial-plan (and Medicaid managed care) tool and does not apply to Medicare, the practice's dominant payer; where it does apply, argue that the limitation is not comparable, never that rates must be equal.

claim: A claim that is denied, appealed, and reversed costs an average of $25 to $118 in staff time to manage ... and is collected 30 to 90 days later
correct_statement: The endpoints are two unrelated, dated estimates: about $25 to rework a claim (MGMA figure cited since at least 2015; $25.20 in a 2021 MGMA article) and $118 per appealed claim (Change Healthcare, 2016 hospital data). Premier's hospital surveys report $43.84 (2022) and $57.23 (2023) per denied claim. No source supports a 30-to-90-day delay.
source_title: MGMA, '4 keys to driving down denials' (Dec. 19, 2018) and MGMA Stat (Mar. 18, 2021); AAFP FPM 2015;22(2):7-10; Premier Inc., 'Claims Adjudication Costs Providers $25.7 Billion' (Feb. 2025)
practice_impact: Fine as a rough argument that prevention beats rework, but do not put $25-$118 or 30-90 days into ROI math; time the practice's own appeals and track days from denial to payment by payer.

claim: Typical % of total denials: Administrative / front-end errors 37, 38%; Medical necessity 22, 23%; Coding and billing errors 17, 18%; Coverage / non-covered service 11, 12%; Coordination of benefits 6, 8%; Timely filing exceeded 4, 5%.
correct_statement: No published source gives this distribution. The closest benchmark, Change Healthcare's 2022 index of hospital claims, shows registration/eligibility 22%, missing or invalid claim data 16%, documentation requests 14%, authorization 13%, service not covered 11%, medical necessity 6%, coding 5%, untimely filing 4%. KFF's 2024 marketplace data put medical necessity at 5% of in-network denials.
source_title: Optum, 'Actionable Insights & Strategies From the Change Healthcare 2022 Denial Index' (HFMA Texas, May 2023); KFF, 'Claims Denials and Appeals in ACA Marketplace Plans in 2024' (Mar. 24, 2026); Massachusetts Health Policy Commission DataPoints on 2024 claim denials
practice_impact: Do not benchmark against this table: its medical-necessity share (22-23%) is about four times published figures and none of the data are physician- or Medicare-specific; build the practice's own mix from remittance CARC/RARC codes by payer.

claim: CY2026 conversion factors are $33.57 (qualifying APM) and $33.40 (non-qualifying APM).
correct_statement: Correct for CY2026: $33.5675 (qualifying APM participants) and $33.4009 (all other clinicians), in force through Dec. 31, 2026. CMS's CY2027 final rule (published Nov. 9, 2026) lowers them to $32.95 and $32.63 on Jan. 1, 2027 (-1.83% and -2.31%) because the one-year 2.5% increase expires.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet: Calendar Year (CY) 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F), Oct. 31, 2025; CY2027 figures from CMS Fact Sheet: CY 2027 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1848-F), Nov. 2026
practice_impact: Benchmark at $33.40 unless clinicians are Qualifying APM Participants; on Jan. 1, 2027 the non-QP factor drops to $32.63, so the fee schedule and every Medicare benchmark must be rebuilt for 2027.

claim: The increase reflects a temporary 2.5% payment bump enacted by Congress through the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a small MACRA statutory update, and a positive budget-neutrality adjustment.
correct_statement: Correct. The CY2026 factors combine MACRA updates of +0.75% (qualifying APM) or +0.25% (others), a one-year +2.5% increase under Public Law 119-21 sec. 71202 (popularly the One Big Beautiful Bill Act; CMS says Working Families Tax Cut legislation) and a +0.49% budget-neutrality adjustment. The 2.5% covers 2026 services only; no enacted extension found as of Nov. 10, 2026.
source_title: CMS Fact Sheet: CY 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule (CMS-1832-F); Public Law 119-21, sec. 71202 (govinfo.gov/content/pkg/PLAW-119publ21/html/PLAW-119publ21.htm); CY 2026 PFS final rule, 90 FR 49960-49961
practice_impact: The 2.5% bump ends Dec. 31, 2026; unless Congress acts, 2027 Medicare payment per RVU falls about 2.3% for non-QP clinicians, which belongs in the 2027 budget.

claim: For Original Medicare, the correct position is to bill above the Medicare allowed amount at the chosen multiplier... if the billed charge is below the Medicare allowed amount, the payment is limited to the billed charge.
correct_statement: Medicare bases payment on the lesser of the actual charge or the fee schedule amount, so a charge below the allowance forfeits money. Participating providers may bill any higher charge. But nonparticipating providers on unassigned claims may not charge above the limiting charge, 115% of the nonpar amount (109.25% of par), so a 200-250% multiplier is unlawful there.
source_title: 42 CFR 414.21 and 414.48 (eCFR, current to Nov. 6, 2026); First Coast Service Options, 'Fee schedule par, nonpar, and limiting charge explanation' and 2026 Florida locality 99 fee schedule; Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 sec. 20
practice_impact: A participating practice loses nothing by charging above the fee schedule; any nonparticipating clinician must cap unassigned Medicare charges at the limiting charge or risk civil penalties up to $19,940 per knowing violation (latest HHS inflation adjustment, 45 CFR 102.3) and exclusion.

claim: The Medicare fee schedule has separate rates for facility settings (hospital outpatient, ASC) and non-facility settings (physician office). The non-facility rate is higher because it includes the practice expense component covering office overhead.
correct_statement: Some PFS codes have separate facility and non-facility rates, set by place-of-service code. Both include practice expense; facility PE RVUs are smaller because the facility bears most direct costs and, since 2026, CMS halves work-based indirect PE. Facility includes hospitals, ASCs and SNF Part A stays (POS 31); nursing facility (POS 32), assisted living and home are non-facility.
source_title: CY 2027 Physician Fee Schedule Final Rule, 91 FR 70992 at 71018-71020 (Nov. 9, 2026), citing Medicare Claims Processing Manual Ch. 12 sec. 20.4.2 (cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Manuals/Downloads/clm104c12.pdf); 42 CFR 414.22(b)(5); CMS 2026 relative value file RVU26D
practice_impact: Nursing-home visits split by POS: in 2026 CPT 99309 is allowed $114.90 in POS 32 but $99.58 in POS 31 (Rest of Florida locality); CMS equalizes 99304-99310 and 99315-99316 on Jan. 1, 2027, so benchmark charges to the higher non-facility rate.

claim: Payment = (Work RVU + Practice Expense RVU + Malpractice RVU) × Geographic Practice Cost Index × Conversion Factor
correct_statement: There is no single GPCI. Payment = [(Work RVU x Work GPCI) + (PE RVU x PE GPCI) + (MP RVU x MP GPCI)] x CF. Each component has its own locality index; 2026 Florida GPCIs (work/PE/MP) are Miami 1.000/1.041/2.529, Fort Lauderdale 1.000/1.013/1.808, Rest of Florida 1.000/0.956/1.503.
source_title: Medicare Claims Processing Manual (Pub. 100-04), Chapter 12, sec. 20.1 Method for Computing Fee Schedule Amount; 42 CFR 414.26(d); CMS CY 2026 GPCI file (Addendum E, RVU26D release)
practice_impact: Florida's malpractice GPCI (1.50-2.53) dwarfs its work and PE indices, so use First Coast's locality fee schedule, not a one-index shortcut; the 1.0 work GPCI floor lapses Jan. 1, 2027 (Rest of Florida 0.977) unless Congress extends it.

claim: Increasing billed charges does not violate payer contracts, practices are generally free to set and adjust their own charges.
correct_statement: Practices generally set their own charges; fee-schedule contracts usually pay the lesser of billed charge or contracted rate, so a uniform increase normally breaches nothing. That is contract-specific (some cap increases or require notice), and law limits charges: Medicare's nonparticipating limiting charge, OIG exclusion authority for Medicare/Medicaid charges substantially above usual charges, and Florida PIP's reasonable-charge rule.
source_title: 42 CFR 1001.701 (OIG permissive exclusion, excessive charges); Fla. Stat. sec. 627.736(5)(a) (2026); 42 CFR 414.48; ECG Management Consultants, 'Capture Every Dollar: Chargemaster Maintenance Strategies for ASC Revenue Growth' (June 5, 2026)
practice_impact: Raise charges uniformly for all payers, read each Medicare Advantage and commercial agreement for charge-related clauses first, and expect no added Medicare revenue: gains arise only where a charge sat below a payer's allowed amount, and non-contracted Medicare Advantage claims stay capped at Original Medicare amounts (42 CFR 422.214).

claim: Contact each major payer's provider relations department and request the current contracted rate schedule. This data is available, payers are contractually required to provide it.
correct_statement: No universal contractual duty exists; access depends on each contract and on state law. Florida requires HMOs, by statute, to disclose the complete schedule of reimbursements to contracted physicians (confidentially); no parallel insurer mandate was found. Commercial plans' in-network rates are public under the federal Transparency in Coverage rule. Medicare Advantage contracts may fall outside both.
source_title: Fla. Stat. sec. 641.315(4)(d) (2026 Florida Statutes); 45 CFR 147.212(b) (Transparency in Coverage); 42 CFR 422.402 (Medicare Advantage preemption); American Medical News, July 31, 2009
practice_impact: Cite s. 641.315(4)(d) when asking HMOs for the full schedule; for other payers rely on the contract, the portal or public machine-readable files, and confirm each Medicare Advantage contract's stated percentage of Medicare.

claim: For most specialties, commercial contracted rates run between 120% and 180% of Medicare.
correct_statement: National averages fit the band: KFF's review found 143% of Medicare (studies ranged 118-179%); MedPAC reports 147% for 2024. But it is not a per-specialty rule: primary care and E/M run about 110-124%, three of 17 studied specialties exceed 180%, and states vary widely (Milliman 2024: 119-243%; HCCI 2017: Florida near 105-110%). The document cites no source.
source_title: MedPAC, Report to the Congress: Medicare Payment Policy (March 2026), Ch. 4; KFF, 'How Much More Than Medicare Do Private Insurers Pay? A Review of the Literature' (2020); Urban Institute (Oct. 2021); HCCI (Aug. 2020); Milliman (June 2024)
practice_impact: Geriatrics is paid mostly by Medicare and Medicare Advantage (MA physician rates ran about 91-102% of traditional Medicare in a 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine study), so few contracts will approach 120-180%; verify actual rates before choosing a multiplier.

claim: Redetermination: the MA plan itself, 60 days to file, plan has 60 days to decide. Reconsideration: Independent Review Entity, 60 days to file after redetermination. ALJ hearing: $190+ claim threshold (2025). Federal Court: $1,900+ threshold (2025).
correct_statement: Part C level 1 is a plan 'reconsideration': file within 65 days of the denial notice; the plan decides in 30 days (pre-service) or 60 days (payment). Adverse decisions go to the IRE automatically. ALJ threshold is $200 for 2026 and 2027; federal court $1,960 for 2026, $2,000 for 2027. Contracted-provider payment disputes follow the contract instead.
source_title: CMS Managed Care Appeals pages (plan reconsideration, IRE, ALJ hearing, federal court; updated 11/03/2026); 42 CFR 422.582, 422.590, 422.600, 422.612; 91 FR 58681 (Sept. 16, 2026); CMS Parts C & D Appeals Guidance (eff. July 6, 2026)
practice_impact: A contracted practice cannot take an MA payment denial to the IRE or an ALJ; it must use the contract's dispute process, and enrollee-side appeals now have a 65-day window.

claim: Common codes like hypertension (I10) carry HCC weight; elevated blood pressure (R03.0) does not.
correct_statement: Essential hypertension (I10) maps to no CMS-HCC payment category in V22, V24 or V28, so it adds nothing to the Part C risk score; it maps only to RxHCC 187 in the Part D drug model. R03.0 maps to no model. Only hypertensive heart-failure or stage 5 CKD combination codes (such as I11.0, I12.0) map to V28 HCCs.
source_title: CMS 2026 Midyear/Final ICD-10-CM Mappings (2026 Model Software/ICD-10 Mappings); identical in 2027 Initial Mappings; 2025 Midyear/Final Mappings for the V24 column
practice_impact: Recapturing I10 on nursing-facility visits will not raise the Part C risk score (only a small Part D RxHCC weight); treating it as an HCC gap misdirects coding audits and shared-savings forecasts.

claim: Type 2 diabetes with diabetic chronic kidney disease (E11.65) has a much higher RAF impact than Type 2 diabetes uncomplicated (E11.9).
correct_statement: E11.65 is type 2 diabetes with hyperglycemia; diabetic CKD is E11.22. Under the V28 model used for all 2026 and 2027 payment, E11.9 and E11.65 both map to HCC 38, and HCCs 36, 37 and 38 share one coefficient (0.166 community non-dual aged, 0.280 institutional). Extra weight requires separately coding the CKD stage (N18.30 to N18.6).
source_title: CMS 2026 Midyear/Final ICD-10-CM Mappings and CMS-HCC V28 model software (relative factors); CY 2026 and CY 2027 Rate Announcements
practice_impact: Diabetes complication specificity alone no longer moves RAF; for long-stay residents the documentable gain is the CKD stage, heart-failure and other separately mapped conditions.
